drugs.name: Isoniazid
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (katG), then blocks mycolic acid synthesis; bactericidal. Resistance: katG mutation. Structurally similar to pyridoxine.
drugs.adverseEffects: Peripheral neuritis from impaired vitamin B6 activation (prevent with pyridoxine 10-50 mg/day); hepatotoxicity from CYP2E1 metabolites, worse with alcohol, rifampin and pyrazinamide; lupus in slow acetylators
drugs.use: Backbone of active TB therapy for all 6 months; taken alone daily for 9 months as one latent TB option; every prescription includes vitamin B6

drugs.name: Rifampin
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; resistance from an altered polymerase. Daily dosing; a strong CYP3A4 inducer; distributes widely into body fluids; covers gram-positive, gram-negative and acid-fast bacteria
drugs.adverseEffects: Red-orange urine, tears and saliva (harmless once blood is excluded; shows adherence); hepatitis, worse with isoniazid or pyrazinamide; induces CYP3A4, so oral contraceptives and HIV drugs fail
drugs.use: Four-drug TB therapy, then continued 4 more months; 4 months alone for latent TB; prophylaxis for close contacts of meningococcal or H. influenzae disease (dorm, jail), not meningitis treatment

drugs.name: Rifabutin
drugs.mechanism: Same RNA polymerase target and red secretions as the parent rifamycin, but much weaker CYP induction; hepatotoxicity similar; reduce the dose when CrCl is below 30 mL/min
drugs.use: Replaces the standard rifamycin in TB patients taking antiretroviral therapy, to avoid induction interactions; optional third drug for MAC in advanced HIV

drugs.name: Rifapentine
drugs.mechanism: Rifamycin RNA polymerase inhibitor with a long half-life that allows once-weekly dosing; still a potent CYP inducer
drugs.use: Weekly with isoniazid for 3 months as a latent TB option in HIV (CD4 < 200); part of the newer 4-month active TB regimen with isoniazid, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin

drugs.name: Pyrazinamide
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug: mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (pncA gene) makes pyrazinoic acid, which lowers intracellular pH and disrupts membranes and fatty acid synthesis; bactericidal on replicating bacilli. Resistance: pncA mutation
drugs.adverseEffects: Marked hepatotoxicity (mitochondrial oxidative stress), additive with isoniazid and rifampin; hyperuricemia from reduced uric acid excretion, which can flare gout
drugs.use: Only the first 2 months (8 weeks) of active TB therapy, then stopped; left out of the pregnancy regimen

drugs.name: Ethambutol
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits mycobacterial arabinosyl transferase (encoded by emb), disrupting the cell envelope; bacteriostatic. Resistance: emb gene mutation
drugs.adverseEffects: Optic neuritis with loss of red-green color discrimination (patients report any vision change); hyperuricemia from increased renal uric acid recovery, which can flare gout
drugs.use: Fourth drug of the 2-month intensive TB phase and kept in the pregnancy regimen; partner to a macrolide for MAC in advanced HIV; also treats M. kansasii

drugs.name: Aminoglycosides (amikacin, streptomycin, gentamicin)
drugs.mechanism: Irreversible 30S binding blocks initiation and causes mRNA misreading; the only bactericidal protein synthesis inhibitors; concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect allow 48-72 h dosing
drugs.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity (nonoliguric acute tubular necrosis; follow BUN and creatinine); ototoxicity of hearing and balance, worse with loop diuretics or cisplatin; neuromuscular blockade in myasthenia; fetal CN VIII damage
drugs.use: Parenteral second-line drug for MDR-TB; plague and tularemia; with ampicillin for a neonatal UTI; added for gram-negative cover in severe HAP; synergy with a beta-lactam against S. aureus

drugs.name: Fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin)
drugs.mechanism: Block DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, so supercoiled DNA cannot relax and reseal; bactericidal. Resistance: altered gyrase, reduced uptake. Inhibit CYP1A2; chelated by antacids, iron and dairy
drugs.adverseEffects: QT prolongation; tendon rupture (older adults, rheumatoid arthritis, glucocorticoids); damage to growing cartilage, so avoided in children and pregnancy; photosensitivity; raise theophylline levels
drugs.use: MDR-TB and the newer 4-month TB regimen; 'respiratory' agents for CAP with comorbidities or admission; anthrax; drug of choice for bacterial prostatitis (2-4 weeks); 3-day course for cystitis

drugs.name: Ethionamide
drugs.mechanism: Blocks mycolic acid synthesis like the first-line cell-wall prodrug, but is activated by the EthA enzyme rather than katG catalase-peroxidase
drugs.use: Second-line TB drug that can still work after isoniazid fails because of a katG mutation

drugs.name: Cycloserine
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits alanine racemase (L-alanine to D-alanine), the cell-wall step before the D-Ala-D-Ala stage; also inhibits GABA transaminase and acts as a partial NMDA agonist
drugs.adverseEffects: Neurologic toxicity: enhanced excitatory glutamate signaling from partial NMDA agonism can provoke seizures; the neurologic effects limit its use
drugs.use: Reserved for multidrug-resistant TB

drugs.name: Linezolid
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 50S subunit (23S rRNA) to block protein synthesis; resistance from a 23S rRNA gene mutation; 100% oral bioavailability, so IV and oral doses are interchangeable
drugs.adverseEffects: Weak MAO inhibition: serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs; bone marrow suppression from impaired mitochondrial ATP production
drugs.use: VRE, MRSA (including MRSA HAP/VAP as the alternative to vancomycin) and penicillin-resistant pneumococcus; the third drug of BPaL for MDR/XDR-TB

drugs.name: Bedaquiline
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, killing both replicating and nonreplicating bacilli; CYP-metabolized (drug interactions); long half-life
drugs.adverseEffects: Boxed warning for QT prolongation, so avoid in long QT; hepatotoxicity from the oxidative stress of its M2 metabolite

drugs.name: Pretomanid
drugs.mechanism: Nitroimidazole prodrug activated by the mycobacterial Ddn nitroreductase; releases nitric oxide and reactive nitrogen species that break down the mycolic acid wall; long half-life
drugs.adverseEffects: Peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation and hepatotoxicity; baseline and regular ECGs and periodic liver tests through the roughly 6-month course
drugs.use: Pulmonary XDR-TB, or MDR-TB that is treatment-intolerant or nonresponsive, given with bedaquiline and linezolid for about 6 months

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.mechanism: Macrolide: binds 50S and blocks translocation; bacteriostatic. Long half-life allows once-daily dosing; no CYP inhibition. Resistance: efflux, 23S rRNA methylation
drugs.use: MAC in advanced HIV (CD4 < 50) with ethambutol; Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila and Legionella pneumonia; pertussis; chlamydia cover beside IM ceftriaxone for gonorrhea; safe in pregnancy and children

drugs.name: Clarithromycin
drugs.mechanism: Macrolide 50S translocation blocker dosed twice daily; inhibits CYP enzymes, so interactions; better absorbed and fewer GI effects than the oldest macrolide
drugs.use: Alternative macrolide partner to ethambutol for MAC; more active against streptococci, staphylococci, H. pylori, Moraxella, Legionella and M. pneumoniae

drugs.name: Erythromycin
drugs.mechanism: The oldest macrolide: 50S translocation block, but needs several doses a day, causes more GI upset and inhibits CYP3A4
drugs.use: Alternative to penicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis in a penicillin-allergic patient

drugs.name: Dapsone
drugs.mechanism: PABA analog that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; bacteriostatic. Resistance: altered dihydropteroate synthase, decreased uptake or increased PABA production
drugs.adverseEffects: Acts like a sulfonamide: hemolysis with bite cells in G6PD deficiency, kernicterus in a neonate, rash up to Stevens-Johnson, crystalluria, interstitial nephritis; cross-allergy with sulfa drugs
drugs.use: Hansen disease (leprosy); Pneumocystis prophylaxis in HIV; topical form for severe acne

drugs.name: Clofazimine
drugs.mechanism: Lipophilic drug with long bactericidal action; binds guanine in mycobacterial DNA and suppresses T lymphocytes (anti-inflammatory); raises reactive oxygen species
drugs.adverseEffects: Pinkish discoloration of skin and conjunctiva; GI upset including GI bleeding; QT prolongation; rare splenic rupture; not used in pregnancy
drugs.use: Hansen disease; not stocked by pharmacies - the physician registers as an investigator with the National Hansen's Disease Program, which supplies it

drugs.name: Thalidomide
drugs.mechanism: Lowers TNF-alpha and decreases angiogenesis; a racemic drug whose (S) enantiomer is the teratogen
drugs.adverseEffects: Short or absent limb long bones (phocomelia) after first-trimester exposure; requires pregnancy tests at the start and during therapy and two forms of birth control
drugs.use: Erythema nodosum leprosum, the severe inflammatory reaction of leprosy; multiple myeloma

drugs.name: Oseltamivir
drugs.mechanism: Oral prodrug; blood and tissue esterases form the active carboxylate, which blocks neuraminidase so new virions clump on the cell surface (influenza A and B); renally secreted, so adjust for renal impairment
drugs.adverseEffects: Nausea and vomiting (taking it with food helps), headache, serious skin reactions; no metabolism-related drug interactions expected
drugs.use: Drug of choice for influenza treatment and prophylaxis at any age, outpatient or inpatient, and in pregnancy; start within 48 hours; twice daily for 5 days

drugs.name: Zanamivir
drugs.mechanism: Neuraminidase inhibitor inhaled as a dry powder; low systemic absorption (about 4-17%), minimal metabolism, no renal dose adjustment listed
drugs.adverseEffects: Bronchospasm in asthma or COPD (an inhaled powder that is not a bronchodilator); headache, sinusitis, dizziness, ear-nose-throat infections; oropharyngeal or facial edema
drugs.use: Outpatient influenza treatment from age 7 and prophylaxis from age 5 in someone who can manage an inhaler; not recommended with underlying airway disease

drugs.name: Peramivir
drugs.mechanism: Neuraminidase inhibitor given intravenously, a single dose for outpatients; excreted unchanged by the kidney (renal dose adjustment); half-life about 20 h
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperglycemia, diarrhea or constipation, serious skin and hypersensitivity reactions; give only where infusion reactions can be treated
drugs.use: Influenza in a patient who cannot take or absorb the oral first-line agent; treatment only, never prophylaxis

drugs.name: Baloxavir marboxil
drugs.mechanism: Prodrug that blocks the influenza PA cap-dependent endonuclease, so the virus cannot snatch capped host primers to start mRNA (A and B); half-life about 80 h, very large Vd; resistance from PA point mutations
drugs.adverseEffects: Headache, diarrhea, nasopharyngitis, hypersensitivity; calcium-containing foods and mineral supplements chelate it in the gut; not recommended in pregnancy for lack of data
drugs.use: One oral dose within 48 h for uncomplicated influenza or post-exposure prophylaxis (age 12+ at risk of complications, 5+ if otherwise healthy); higher BMI needs a higher dose

drugs.name: Amantadine
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the influenza A M2 proton channel, preventing uncoating; enters the CNS well; excreted about 90% unchanged in urine; half-life 12-18 h in young adults, 29 h in older adults, 8 days in ESRD and not dialyzable
drugs.adverseEffects: Difficulty concentrating, agitation, insomnia, confusion and hallucinations, especially in the elderly; worse with antihistamines and psychotropic or anticholinergic drugs
drugs.use: No longer used for influenza (high-level resistance, influenza A only); still used for Parkinson disease symptoms

drugs.name: Rimantadine
drugs.mechanism: M2 proton channel blocker (influenza A only) with low CNS distribution and extensive hepatic hydroxylation and conjugation; excreted as metabolites; half-life highly variable (13-65 h)
drugs.adverseEffects: CNS effects such as insomnia and poor concentration occur less often than with its brain-penetrating relative

drugs.name: Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir (Paxlovid)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease, so viral polyproteins are not cleaved; the co-packaged pill inhibits CYP3A4 so the antiviral is not inactivated (pharmacokinetic booster)
drugs.adverseEffects: Bad taste (dysgeusia), nausea, diarrhea, rash; liver enzyme rise and hypersensitivity from the booster; boxed warning for major CYP3A4 drug-drug interactions; renal dose adjustment
drugs.use: Preferred oral antiviral for mild-moderate COVID-19 in a high-risk outpatient (12+), within 5 days of symptoms after an interaction check; no second course for rebound

drugs.name: Remdesivir
drugs.mechanism: Adenosine nucleotide analog prodrug, triphosphorylated and incorporated by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; the chain stops two or three nucleotides later (delayed chain termination)
drugs.adverseEffects: Severe bradycardia (mechanism unknown); reversible aminotransferase rise; hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, angioedema; hyperglycemia; chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine lowers its effect
drugs.use: IV for COVID-19 in hospitalized patients not on mechanical ventilation (usually 5 days) or high-risk outpatients (3 days); infants of 3 kg and up; only where infusion reactions can be treated

drugs.name: Molnupiravir
drugs.mechanism: Oral prodrug of NHC; the viral RdRp takes up NHC triphosphate in place of cytidine or uridine, so copies pile up mutations until the RNA is nonviable (lethal mutagenesis, viral error catastrophe)
drugs.adverseEffects: Rash, hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis; teratogenicity and fetal loss in animals (contraception during and 4 days after); bone and cartilage growth concerns under 18
drugs.use: Alternative oral agent for mild-moderate COVID-19 in high-risk adults when the preferred agent cannot be used; shortens recovery but does not reduce hospitalization

drugs.name: Tecovirimat
drugs.mechanism: Stops newly made orthopoxvirus particles from being released from infected cells
drugs.use: FDA-approved for smallpox; used off-label for severe mpox alongside supportive care and pain control

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.mechanism: Glycopeptide that binds the D-alanine-D-alanine end of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking cell wall polymer assembly after the alanine racemase step; resistance now seen in E. faecium and some S. aureus
drugs.use: IV for MRSA, including MRSA HAP/VAP; given orally, with fidaxomicin as the other first-line choice, for C. difficile colitis; with imipenem and an aminoglycoside for severe HAP

drugs.name: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)
drugs.mechanism: Sequential folate blockade: the sulfonamide (a PABA analog) inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and its partner inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so no tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis
drugs.use: 3 days for uncomplicated cystitis (10-14 if complicated); drug of choice for Pneumocystis pneumonia; sinusitis or epiglottitis in penicillin allergy or suspected S. aureus

drugs.name: Penicillin and aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin)
drugs.mechanism: Beta-lactams that inhibit the transpeptidases (PBPs) cross-linking peptidoglycan; useless against wall-less Mycoplasma and against MRSA's mecA-encoded PBP2a; clavulanate added against beta-lactamase
drugs.use: Strep pharyngitis with 4 Centor points (no test needed); first-line bacterial sinusitis and healthy-outpatient CAP; actinomycosis; 7 days for bacteriuria in pregnancy; neonatal UTI with gentamicin

drugs.name: Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime)
drugs.mechanism: Beta-lactam transpeptidase (PBP) inhibitors with broad gram-negative reach; resistance now spreading in E. coli, K. pneumoniae and gonococci; enterococci are intrinsically resistant
drugs.use: Empiric bacterial meningitis; IM dose for gonorrhea; febrile infant UTI (IM or IV); epiglottitis; inpatient CAP with a macrolide; acute pyelonephritis

drugs.name: Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem)
drugs.mechanism: Strongest beta-lactams; Enterobacterales resist them via efflux pumps, lower outer-membrane permeability and, above all, KPC, NDM and VIM carbapenemases that clavulanate barely blocks
drugs.use: Last-resort agents for resistant Klebsiella, E. coli and Pseudomonas; antipseudomonal choice for HAP/VAP; kept in combination regimens for resistant Enterobacterales when the MIC is 4 or less

drugs.name: Doxycycline (tetracyclines)
drugs.mechanism: Binds the 30S subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment, so the peptide chain cannot elongate; bacteriostatic; binds divalent and trivalent cations
drugs.adverseEffects: Binds calcium in growing bone and teeth: irreversible tooth staining and effects on growth, so not used in pregnancy or young children
drugs.use: Q fever; Mycoplasma pneumonia (no cell wall, so beta-lactams fail); outpatient CAP in a patient without comorbidities

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.mechanism: Nitroimidazole that generates nitrogen free radicals; the newer nitroimidazole for drug-resistant TB was built on the same chemistry
drugs.use: Anaerobic coverage, paired with a beta-lactam, for aspiration pneumonia; second line for C. difficile colitis after oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin

drugs.name: Amphotericin B
drugs.mechanism: Binds ergosterol, the sterol fungal membranes use in place of cholesterol, disrupting the membrane; Candida lusitaniae and C. guilliermondii resist it
drugs.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, additive with aminoglycosides and cisplatin; low selective toxicity because fungal and human cells are both eukaryotic, so side effects are common
drugs.use: Severe or disseminated endemic mycoses, including talaromycosis; with flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis; with surgical debridement for mucormycosis; disseminated candidiasis

drugs.name: Albuterol (SABA)
drugs.mechanism: Inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle within minutes; the effect lasts only a few hours
drugs.use: Rescue inhaler for acute symptoms in asthma and in every COPD group; puffs before exercise for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction; given during spirometry to test reversibility (12% and 200 mL)

drugs.name: LABA (salmeterol)
drugs.mechanism: Long-acting inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist: 12 hours or more of bronchodilation, so it is a maintenance drug, not a rescue drug
drugs.use: With an inhaled corticosteroid for asthma maintenance; in COPD alone for GOLD group A or combined with a long-acting muscarinic antagonist for groups B and E

drugs.name: LAMA / SAMA (tiotropium, ipratropium)
drugs.mechanism: Block M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle, removing vagal cholinergic bronchoconstriction; long-acting forms last about 24 hours
drugs.use: COPD maintenance alone for GOLD group A or paired with a long-acting beta-2 agonist for groups B and E; the short-acting form is a COPD rescue option alongside albuterol

drugs.name: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)
drugs.adverseEffects: Oral thrush (oropharyngeal candidiasis): the patient should rinse the mouth after every dose
drugs.use: Asthma maintenance, combined with a LABA; the combination can now also serve as rescue; certain ones are acceptable in pregnancy

drugs.name: Montelukast
drugs.mechanism: Blocks leukotriene receptors, countering the leukotriene rise that follows COX-1 inhibition (less PGE2, more leukotrienes, mucosal edema)
drugs.use: Asthma with nasal polyps that worsens 20 minutes to 3 hours after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs

drugs.name: Omalizumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against IgE, so less IgE arms the high-affinity receptors on mast cells that allergens cross-link to release histamine
drugs.use: Specialist-started add-on for severe allergic (IgE-mediated) asthma that stays uncontrolled despite adherence, good inhaler technique and a confirmed diagnosis

drugs.name: Mepolizumab / reslizumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibodies against IL-5, the cytokine that recruits eosinophils into the airway
drugs.use: Specialist-started add-on for severe eosinophil-driven asthma that stays uncontrolled despite adherence, good inhaler technique and a confirmed diagnosis

drugs.name: Heliox
drugs.mechanism: Helium mixed with oxygen is less dense than air, so it gets past severely narrowed, swollen airways with less resistance
drugs.use: Status asthmaticus not responding to IV steroids, inhaled beta-2 agonists and IV magnesium, as a bridge while CPAP/BiPAP or intubation is considered

drugs.name: Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone)
drugs.adverseEffects: Suppress host defenses, raising the risk of invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients; a cause of metabolic alkalosis
drugs.use: IV in status asthmaticus; oral, with albuterol, for a COPD exacerbation; first line for progressive sarcoidosis; desquamative interstitial pneumonia and eosinophilic pneumonias

drugs.name: Supplemental O2
drugs.adverseEffects: In a chronic CO2 retainer, too much can push PaCO2 higher and depress breathing (taught as loss of hypoxic drive), so titrate to a modest saturation
drugs.use: The one COPD therapy proven to improve mortality and survival; in an exacerbation, give only enough to correct the hypoxemia

drugs.name: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
drugs.mechanism: Block the renin-angiotensin system, lowering intraglomerular pressure and hyperfiltration, which slows CKD progression
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia and a creatinine rise: recheck creatinine and potassium 2-4 weeks after starting or changing the dose; with ACE blockade, a dry cough for months that can also worsen incontinence
drugs.use: Diabetic CKD once proteinuria appears, and to slow CKD in general; avoid in stage 4-5 CKD and renal artery stenosis; guidelines often have them held before iodinated contrast

drugs.name: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
drugs.mechanism: Block sodium-glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule, lowering blood glucose and reducing glomerular hyperfiltration
drugs.use: Slow CKD progression (strongest evidence alongside RAS blockade); in CKD with heart failure they help regardless of albuminuria; in type 2 diabetes, fewer cardiovascular events and weight loss

drugs.name: Thiazide diuretics
drugs.mechanism: Block the NaCl cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule and increase distal calcium reabsorption, so less calcium reaches the urine
drugs.use: Prevent recurrent calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones, with a low-sodium (not low-calcium) diet; stopped at least 24 h before iodinated contrast

drugs.name: Potassium citrate
drugs.mechanism: Complexes calcium in the urine, lowering calcium saturation, crystal growth and aggregation; the body's own stone inhibitor is low in renal tubular acidosis, strenuous exercise and high-animal-protein diets
drugs.use: Calcium phosphate stones, alongside a low-sodium diet and a thiazide

drugs.name: Allopurinol
drugs.mechanism: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor: less uric acid is made, so less reaches the urine
drugs.use: Prevents and treats radiolucent stones that form when urine pH is below 5.5, together with fluids and urine alkalinization

drugs.name: Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin)
drugs.mechanism: Block smooth-muscle adrenergic receptors: less ureteral spasm, more pressure above a stone, a relaxed ureter at and below it; also lower the raised adrenergic tone of prostatic and urethral muscle
drugs.adverseEffects: Urethral relaxation can cause or worsen urinary leakage, so they appear on the list of drugs that cause incontinence
drugs.use: Medical expulsive therapy for a ureteral stone larger than 5 mm and up to 10 mm, with pain control and straining the urine

drugs.name: Tiopronin / penicillamine
drugs.mechanism: Chelating agents that bind cystine and help dissolve the stones
drugs.use: Inherited stone disease with hexagonal crystals that keeps recurring despite a low-sodium diet, high fluids and urine alkalinization

drugs.name: NSAIDs (ketorolac, ibuprofen)
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective COX inhibition blocks prostaglandin synthesis, so the kidney loses vasodilatory prostaglandins; COX-2-selective drugs spare the gut but still affect the COX-2-rich kidney
drugs.adverseEffects: Ischemic AKI with papillary necrosis at high doses; hypersensitivity interstitial nephritis, sometimes with minimal change nephrotic syndrome; hyperkalemia in CKD; bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma
drugs.use: First-line analgesic for renal colic (opioids only occasionally, e.g. significant renal impairment); avoided in CKD and stopped 24-48 h before iodinated contrast

drugs.name: Oxybutynin / tolterodine
drugs.mechanism: Anticholinergics that block muscarinic receptors on the detrusor, damping the involuntary contractions of an overactive bladder
drugs.adverseEffects: Dry mouth, constipation, dry eyes, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, fast heart rate; cross the blood-brain barrier (caution in the elderly); avoid in heart disease and closed-angle glaucoma
drugs.use: Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity after lifestyle measures; the urge component of mixed incontinence

drugs.name: Vaginal / topical estrogen
drugs.mechanism: Restores the hormone-dependent support of the bladder neck and urethral tissues that weakens after menopause ('plumps the area back up')
drugs.use: Stress incontinence in a perimenopausal or recently postmenopausal woman; cream for symptomatic labial adhesions in a girl, for 2-3 weeks until they separate

drugs.name: OnabotulinumtoxinA (botulinum toxin)
drugs.mechanism: Injected into the detrusor, it blocks acetylcholine release and relaxes the bladder
drugs.adverseEffects: Can paralyze the bladder, so the patient may have to self-catheterize
drugs.use: Urge incontinence that persists despite lifestyle change and anticholinergic drugs; sacral nerve modulation and bladder augmentation are the other later options

drugs.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
drugs.mechanism: Synthetic vasopressin analog that concentrates the urine and cuts nighttime urine production; it controls bedwetting but does not cure it
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyponatremia, especially in elderly patients on other medications, sometimes enough to need admission
drugs.use: Primary nocturnal enuresis when dry nights matter, such as sleepovers (the bed-wetting alarm is the cure); nighttime incontinence in adults, with caution

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.mechanism: Extra buffer outside cells pulls H+ out in exchange for K+ moving in; used to alkalinize the urine (not the serum), so some toxins leave faster and some stones form less readily
drugs.adverseEffects: Not for DKA (worse outcomes in studies), rhabdomyolysis (fewer myoglobin casts but no AKI or mortality benefit) or simply an unwanted pH number
drugs.use: Hyperkalemia; tricyclic and other Na+ channel blocker overdose; urine alkalinization in salicylate overdose; oral alkali in CKD acidosis to keep serum HCO3- above 23

drugs.name: Acetazolamide
drugs.mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: bicarbonate is lost in the urine, producing a metabolic acidosis that drives ventilation up
drugs.use: Prophylaxis before a high-altitude ascent; very severe metabolic alkalosis; considered when respiratory alkalosis dominates early salicylate poisoning

drugs.name: Fomepizole
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, so ethylene glycol and methanol are converted to their toxic acids slowly enough for the liver to cope
drugs.use: Antidote for antifreeze or methanol poisoning; without it, IV (or even oral) ethanol competes for the enzyme; add thiamine and pyridoxine, and dialysis in severe cases

genes.name: Asthma
genes.gene: IL-4/5/9/13 cluster, beta-adrenergic and glucocorticoid receptor genes
genes.role: Susceptibility locus linked to total IgE and atopy; 12q is the other locus taught, for atopy and airway hyperresponsiveness

genes.name: Familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
genes.role: Inherited telomerase defects (about 15% of familial cases) shorten telomeres, so alveolar epithelial cells die and cannot regenerate

genes.name: Familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
genes.role: Other telomere-maintenance genes found mutated in affected families, alongside the two telomerase-component genes

genes.name: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
genes.role: Mucin gene variant that raises mucus secretion and alters mucociliary clearance; present in about one third of cases

genes.name: Familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
genes.role: Encoded by SFTPC; surfactant-gene mutations cause rare familial forms, and SP-C is one of the factors that affect telomere length and function

genes.name: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis
genes.role: Found in some smokers in their late 30s to early 40s with grooved, CD1a-positive cells; symptoms usually fade after quitting

genes.name: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (hereditary)
genes.role: Macrophages need GM-CSF signaling to clear surfactant; 90% of cases are instead autoimmune, with antibodies against GM-CSF

genes.name: Lung adenocarcinoma
genes.role: Gain-of-function kinase mutation in about 15%, typical of women who never smoked; specific kinase inhibitors prolong survival

genes.name: Lung adenocarcinoma
genes.role: In about 30%, more often in smokers; usually a worse prognosis, with targeted treatment still emerging

genes.name: Lung adenocarcinoma
genes.role: Receptor tyrosine kinase genes listed with EGFR, MET and RET as gain-of-function drivers of the glandular, TTF-1-positive type

genes.name: Small cell lung carcinoma
genes.gene: TP53 and RB1 loss of function
genes.role: Both tumor suppressors lost in this neuroendocrine tumor with the strongest tie to smoking

genes.name: Small cell lung carcinoma
genes.role: MYC-family amplification joins the two tumor-suppressor losses in the chromogranin- and synaptophysin-positive tumor

genes.name: Squamous cell lung carcinoma
genes.gene: TP53 mutation (highest rate of any lung cancer type)
genes.role: The single most important gene for this central, keratinizing, smoking-related tumor

genes.name: Squamous cell lung carcinoma
genes.role: Cell-cycle brake lost in most of these keratinizing tumors, alongside p53

genes.name: Squamous cell lung carcinoma
genes.role: Growth factor receptor gain in the central, PTHrP-secreting tumor type

genes.name: Malignant mesothelioma
genes.role: About 80% delete this region and lose the tumor suppressor; the pleural tumor encases the lung decades after the exposure

genes.name: Malignant mesothelioma
genes.role: Further tumor-suppressor mutations found beside the common 9p loss in the pleural tumor that follows occupational fiber exposure

genes.name: Solitary fibrous tumor of the pleura
genes.role: Unique fusion in a usually benign, pedunculated, keratin-negative mass that has nothing to do with asbestos

genes.name: Alport syndrome
genes.role: Alpha-5 chain of GBM type IV collagen: underproduction and faulty network assembly; hematuria with hearing loss and eye findings, onset at 5-20 years

genes.name: Alport syndrome
genes.role: Alpha-3 chain of GBM type IV collagen; the less common recessive form of the same collagen disease with hearing and eye involvement

genes.name: Thin basement membrane disease
genes.role: Alpha-3 or alpha-4 collagen chain change, dominant inheritance: hematuria runs in the family, without hearing or eye loss or familial kidney failure

genes.name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
genes.gene: ADAMTS13 mutation (inherited; less common than autoantibody)
genes.role: Metalloproteinase that trims von Willebrand factor multimers; most cases are acquired autoantibodies, treated with plasma exchange

genes.name: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
genes.role: About half of cases: complement activation goes unchecked and injures endothelium, with no diarrheal prodrome and a worse course

genes.name: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
genes.gene: Complement factor I or CD46 (membrane cofactor protein) mutation
genes.role: Loss of another complement regulator, the explanation in patients without the commoner regulator defect

genes.name: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
genes.role: Tumor suppressor that normally targets HIF-1; with it gone, HIF-1 drives VEGF and angiogenesis in this proximal tubule tumor

genes.name: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
genes.gene: Germline VHL tumor suppressor mutation (autosomal dominant)
genes.role: Renal cysts and bilateral clear cell tumors with cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas and pheochromocytoma

genes.name: Papillary renal cell carcinoma
genes.gene: Trisomies 7, 16 and 17; loss of Y in men (sporadic)
genes.role: Distal convoluted tubule tumor with foamy macrophages in its fibrovascular cores; the commonest kidney cancer in dialysis patients

genes.name: Hereditary papillary renal cell carcinoma
genes.role: Autosomal dominant gain of the growth-factor receptor gene, giving multiple bilateral tumors

genes.name: Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma
genes.role: Genetically distinct subtype of young patients; clear cytoplasm with papillary architecture

genes.name: Tuberous sclerosis
genes.gene: TSC1 or TSC2 loss of function (autosomal dominant)
genes.role: Tumor suppressors that together restrain mTOR; renal angiomyolipomas in 25-50%, cardiac rhabdomyomas, retinal hamartomas, skin angiofibromas

genes.name: WAGR syndrome
genes.role: About 33% develop a childhood renal embryonal tumor; absent irises, genital anomalies and developmental delay come with the deletion

genes.name: Denys-Drash syndrome
genes.role: About 90% develop a childhood renal embryonal tumor; with gonadal dysgenesis and renal failure from diffuse mesangial sclerosis

genes.name: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
genes.role: Organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele and enlarged adrenals, with raised childhood renal tumor risk

genes.name: Wilms tumor with focal anaplasia
genes.role: Seen in the undifferentiated, pleomorphic areas; these children tend to resist chemotherapy
avoid: Invasive urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis

genes.name: Noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma
genes.gene: FGFR3 amplification with activating RAS and PI3-kinase mutations
genes.role: Gain in growth factor receptor signaling; these tumors recur often but progress to muscle invasion in only about 20%

genes.name: Urothelial carcinoma in situ (flat pathway)
genes.role: High-grade, multifocal, confined to the epithelium at first, yet the precursor of most muscle-invasive bladder cancer

genes.name: Superficial urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
genes.role: Seen in noninvasive tumors of the pelvicalyceal lining; smoking is the big risk factor

genes.name: Invasive urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
genes.role: Marks the tumors that have grown beyond the lining of the upper collecting system

correlates.name: Isoniazid hepatotoxicity
correlates.presentation: 52-year-old man who drinks 6 beers a day; positive IGRA before adalimumab, so he began one daily oral drug plus pyridoxine 7 weeks ago for a planned 9 months. 1 week of nausea, anorexia, dark urine and right upper quadrant ache; T 37.4 C, scleral icterus, tender liver edge
correlates.workup: ALT 840 U/L, AST 710 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L, total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, INR 1.3; hepatitis A, B and C serologies negative; liver tests were normal at baseline
correlates.management: Stop the drug at once; trend liver tests and INR; no alcohol; refer for transplant evaluation if liver failure develops. Prevention: baseline and periodic liver tests, extra caution with alcohol or when given with rifampin and pyrazinamide

correlates.name: Isoniazid peripheral neuropathy
correlates.presentation: 50-year-old woman 6 weeks into four-drug therapy for cavitary pulmonary TB; no vitamin supplement was prescribed. 2 weeks of burning and numbness in both feet, worse at night. Vitals normal, lungs clear, decreased pinprick sensation over the toes; vision and color testing normal
correlates.management: Add pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 10-50 mg/day and continue TB therapy; B6 belongs on every prescription of the katG-activated drug, which blocks B6 activation and so lowers glutamate-to-GABA conversion

correlates.name: Serotonin syndrome from linezolid and an SSRI
correlates.presentation: 34-year-old woman on sertraline for depression began an oral antibiotic 2 days ago for vancomycin-resistant enterococcal bacteremia. Now agitated, sweating, with diarrhea; T 39.6 C, HR 128, BP 150/90; tremor, myoclonic jerks, brisk reflexes and sustained ankle clonus
correlates.management: Treat as an emergency: stop both serotonergic drugs, cool and give benzodiazepines for agitation as needed, and start cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist)

correlates.name: Thalidomide embryopathy
correlates.presentation: Newborn of a 24-year-old woman from Brazil treated for leprosy; she took an oral TNF-lowering, anti-angiogenic drug for painful red skin nodules in the first trimester, before she knew she was pregnant. Hands arise near the shoulders; long bones of all four limbs short or absent
correlates.management: Prevention: negative pregnancy tests before and during therapy and two forms of birth control for any patient who could conceive; never use the drug for first-trimester morning sickness

correlates.name: Zanamivir bronchospasm
correlates.presentation: 45-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 55% predicted) and 1 day of fever, myalgia and dry cough took his first dose of an inhaled dry-powder influenza antiviral. Within 30 minutes: chest tightness, RR 26, SpO2 88% on room air, prolonged expiration with diffuse wheezes
correlates.management: Stop the inhaled powder and give a short-acting bronchodilator; switch to oral oseltamivir. This inhaled antiviral is not recommended in asthma or COPD

correlates.name: Neuraminidase-inhibitor neuropsychiatric events
correlates.presentation: 11-year-old boy with rapid-antigen-positive influenza started a twice-daily oral antiviral suspension yesterday. Tonight he is confused and frightened, sees insects on the wall and tried to run outside. T 38.4 C, HR 110, neck supple, no focal deficits; it clears within hours
correlates.management: Stop the drug and observe him in a safe setting; these reactions are rare, transient and of unestablished cause, mostly in children and adolescents, and came to light in post-marketing surveillance

correlates.name: Amantadine neurotoxicity
correlates.presentation: 80-year-old man with Parkinson disease on hemodialysis for ESRD takes a renally cleared antiparkinsonian drug at his usual dose; diphenhydramine was added for sleep. Over 1 day he is suddenly not making sense, agitated and hallucinating. T 36.8 C, no focal deficits
correlates.management: Stop the drug and the antihistamine and support him while it clears slowly (half-life about 8 days in ESRD; dialysis does not remove it). Sudden onset in an older patient: think drug, not age
